latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Insufficient CD4 T-cell, macrophage, and lymphocyte-mediated clearance permits Pneumocystis jirovecii persistence and replication in alveoli. This mechanism is modulated by HIV, glucocorticoids, transplant immunosuppression, malignancy, lymphocyte-depleting therapy, and prophylaxis status rather than being a disease-name subtype.

Burden of Pneumocystis trophic forms and cysts attached to type I pneumocytes and present in alveolar spaces. High burden drives diagnostic PCR/stain positivity and beta-D-glucan release; it falls only with active anti-Pneumocystis therapy or restored cellular immunity.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Foamy alveolar exudate and surfactant dysfunction
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Proteinaceous foamy alveolar material, organism forms, and surfactant disruption thicken the diffusion barrier and create patchy airspace filling without the dense lobar neutrophilic consolidation typical of bacterial pneumonia.

Macrophage and lymphocyte cytokine response to Pneumocystis antigens and beta-glucan. In HIV it may evolve subacutely with high organism burden; in non-HIV immunocompromised hosts it can be abrupt, lower-burden, and more injurious.
Diffuse or patchy bilateral interstitial and alveolar injury producing ground-glass opacities, often perihilar or upper-lobe predominant, sometimes with a normal early chest radiograph.

Impaired gas exchange from interstitial thickening, foamy exudate, surfactant dysfunction, and inflammatory alveolitis. Hypoxemia is often disproportionate to auscultatory findings and can be revealed by exertion early.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cystic lung injury and air-leak pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Subpleural cysts, pneumatoceles, and fragile injured lung regions create risk of spontaneous pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum, especially with advanced disease or positive pressure ventilation.

Restoration of cellular immunity after ART initiation or reduction of iatrogenic immunosuppression can transiently amplify pulmonary inflammation after organism control has begun. This is a context-dependent mechanism, not a separate disease leaf.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Loss of CD4/macrophage clearance permits progressive organism accumulation in alveoli.
Organism accumulation and alveolar attachment generate foamy proteinaceous exudate and surfactant dysfunction.
Pneumocystis antigens and beta-glucan activate macrophage and lymphocyte inflammatory signaling.
Foamy alveolar filling and surfactant impairment produce the CT ground-glass pattern.
Inflammatory alveolitis thickens septa and worsens diffuse interstitial opacity.
Diffuse lung injury raises diffusion distance and V/Q mismatch, lowering PaO2 and oxygen saturation.
Alveolar filling and interstitial involvement create visible infiltrate burden.
Ground-glass opacity is the core CT expression of PJP lung injury.
PJP often shows diffuse, perihilar, or upper-lobe predominant ground-glass opacity, especially in atypical prophylaxis contexts.
Pneumocystis cyst walls contain beta-D-glucan; serum levels are sensitive but not specific.
PCR positivity scales with respiratory organism nucleic acid burden but may not alone separate colonization from disease.
BAL staining or immunofluorescence detects organism forms when burden and sample quality are sufficient.
LDH rises with diffuse lung tissue injury; it is common but nonspecific.
Fever follows pulmonary cytokine activation, though glucocorticoids or profound immunosuppression may blunt it.
CRP may rise with lung inflammation, but values overlap with other pneumonias and can be blunted by immunosuppression.
PJP alone often has low or modest procalcitonin compared with bacterial pneumonia; marked elevation suggests coinfection.
Hypoxemia is the characteristic physiologic abnormality and may appear first with exertion.
P/F ratio captures severity of oxygenation failure across oxygen support levels.
An elevated A-a gradient is a canonical PJP severity marker and treatment context axis for corticosteroids.
Tachypnea compensates for diffusion-limited hypoxemia and rising work of breathing.
Progressive exertional dyspnea follows reduced oxygen transfer and increased respiratory drive.
Interstitial and alveolar irritation produces dry or minimally productive cough.
Many PJP presentations evolve over days to weeks rather than hours, particularly in HIV-associated disease.
Exercise desaturation can reveal early diffusion impairment even when resting oxygen saturation is near normal.
PJP can produce cysts or pneumatoceles that become visible on CT.
Fragile cystic lung changes and positive pressure ventilation increase pneumothorax risk.
Spontaneous pneumothorax is a recognized PJP complication and should raise suspicion in immunocompromised hosts.
Severe PJP can progress to diffuse inflammatory lung injury meeting ARDS physiology.
Severe hypoxemia and work of breathing can require intubation; invasive ventilation marks high risk.
Respiratory symptom recurrence after immune restoration can reflect PJP-associated IRIS after exclusion of other causes.
Restored cellular immunity can amplify residual pulmonary inflammation.
Respiratory failure is the dominant proximate mortality pathway in PJP.
Pneumothorax complicates ventilation and worsens gas exchange, increasing death risk.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: ICU care, corticosteroids, or broad immunosuppression
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Severe lung injury, ICU exposure, and immunosuppression increase bacterial, viral, and fungal coinfection risk.

axes.shape_free_text: Fever is common but may be low-grade or blunted by glucocorticoids and profound immunosuppression.
Sinus tachycardia tracks fever, hypoxemia, and respiratory distress.
Tachypnea is frequent and may be more prominent than auscultatory findings.
Resting SpO2 can be normal early but falls with progression; exertional decline is an early clue.
Falls as diffusion limitation and V/Q mismatch progress; severe disease can be below 200 and ARDS-like below 100.
A-a oxygen gradient rises early; values >=35 mmHg indicate moderate or worse oxygenation impairment in common PJP severity frameworks.
0 none, 1 low-flow oxygen, 2 high-flow oxygen, 3 noninvasive ventilation, 4 invasive ventilation, 5 extracorporeal support.
Progressive exertional then resting dyspnea is a dominant symptom.
Dry or minimally productive cough is typical; purulent sputum suggests bacterial coinfection.
Drop in oxygen saturation during ambulation or minimal exercise before marked resting hypoxemia.
Chest discomfort can occur but sharp pleuritic pain should raise concern for pneumothorax or alternate pathology.
Fine diffuse crackles may be present, though resting lung examination may be normal in mild disease.
Respiratory symptoms often evolve over 7-28 days; non-HIV immunocompromised hosts may present more abruptly.
Malaise and fatigue often accompany subacute respiratory symptoms.
Rash is not a core PJP finding, but is an important treatment-toxicity and sulfonamide-reaction observation.
Diarrhea is a nonspecific symptom and treatment-tolerability axis for oral anti-Pneumocystis alternatives.
WBC may be normal, low from underlying immunosuppression, or elevated with coinfection or steroids.
Lymphopenia supports impaired cell-mediated immunity and is associated with worse non-HIV outcomes.
Low CD4 count is a major susceptibility context; counts below 200 cells/uL strongly increase PJP risk in HIV and other T-cell deficient states.
Often elevated from lung injury; high values correlate with severity but are nonspecific.
Sensitive fungal cell-wall marker in PJP but not specific; low values argue against PJP in many contexts.
Usually elevated but variable; very high values or neutrophilia increase concern for coinfection.
Often low or modest in isolated PJP; marked elevation suggests bacterial coinfection or sepsis.
Platelets are usually not a primary PJP discriminator, but thrombocytopenia affects differential diagnosis and anti-Pneumocystis drug toxicity monitoring.
ALT is usually normal or mildly abnormal in isolated PJP, but is important for drug toxicity and alternative diagnosis context.
Hypoalbuminemia reflects chronic illness and severity but is not specific to PJP.
Baseline renal function is central for TMP-SMX and pentamidine toxicity and dosing; disease itself usually affects creatinine indirectly through severity or drugs.
Parent CT/CXR infiltrate presence and extent axis. A normal early CXR does not exclude PJP; CT is more sensitive.
Satellite of infiltrate presence: bilateral patchy or diffuse ground-glass attenuation is the core CT pattern.
Satellite distribution descriptor for PJP ground-glass opacity; perihilar or upper-lobe patterns are supportive but not required.
Satellite CT descriptor for cysts, pneumatoceles, or blebs that increase air-leak risk.
Satellite complication finding; spontaneous pneumothorax in an immunocompromised patient should raise PJP suspicion.
Pleural effusion is usually absent or small in isolated PJP; prominent effusion suggests alternative or concurrent pathology.
Respiratory sample PCR probability; highly sensitive but must be interpreted with organism load and clinical disease probability.
BAL stain or immunofluorescence positivity probability; specificity is high when organisms are visualized.
Induced sputum diagnostic yield is variable and lower than BAL; a negative result does not exclude disease when pretest probability is high.
Context axis for whether the current regimen has active anti-Pneumocystis effect at adequate exposure.
Pragmatic active-drug context for TMP-SMX response; true clinical susceptibility testing is not routinely available.
History of severe sulfonamide reaction such as SJS/TEN, DRESS, or severe organ toxicity that prevents TMP-SMX rechallenge.
G6PD deficiency increases hemolysis and methemoglobinemia risk with dapsone and primaquine.
Renal impairment requiring dosing adjustment or intensified toxicity monitoring.
Advanced renal dysfunction increases TMP-SMX and pentamidine toxicity and complicates dosing.
Pregnancy modifies risk-benefit for TMP-SMX, primaquine, dapsone, pentamidine, and folate supplementation.
Baseline or acquired QTc-prolongation risk modifies macrolide, fluoroquinolone, and pentamidine safety in PJP mimics or coinfection coverage.
Risk of serious hyperglycemia, psychiatric toxicity, or other glucocorticoid harm modifies adjunctive steroid risk-benefit.
Ability to absorb oral therapy reliably; low values weaken atovaquone, dapsone/TMP, and primaquine-containing regimens.
Methemoglobinemia can occur with dapsone or primaquine and causes persistent hypoxemia despite pulmonary improvement.
Baseline and treatment-emergent anemia affect oxygen delivery; hemolysis risk rises with dapsone or primaquine in G6PD deficiency.
TMP-SMX can raise potassium; pentamidine can also cause electrolyte abnormalities.
Corticosteroids and pentamidine can cause clinically important dysglycemia.
Composite context for impaired host defense; should be decomposed when CD4, transplant, glucocorticoid, chemotherapy, or biologic details are available.
Context axis for advanced HIV-related cellular immunodeficiency; not a disease-name constraint.
Corticosteroid, transplant, chemotherapy, or biologic immunosuppression intensity that raises risk and may be reduced if clinically feasible.
Degree of active PJP prophylaxis before disease onset or after treatment; lowers prior probability and recurrence hazard but does not exclude breakthrough disease.
Hazard of transition to ARDS physiology from diffuse inflammatory lung injury.
Hazard of needing invasive ventilation from refractory hypoxemia or work of breathing.
Hazard of pneumothorax or air leak from cystic lung injury, especially with positive pressure ventilation.
Hazard of paradoxical pulmonary inflammatory worsening after immune restoration, after excluding persistent infection or alternative diagnoses.
Hazard of bacterial, viral, or fungal coinfection during severe disease, ICU care, or intensified immunosuppression.
Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from oxygenation failure, ARDS, pneumothorax, coinfection, host frailty, and treatment toxicity context.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Falling oxygen saturation increases respiratory drive and tachypnea.
Both measure oxygenation impairment from the same gas-exchange pathology.
Both rise with organism burden but differ by sampling site and false-positive contexts.
Higher LDH reflects lung injury and often accompanies worse oxygenation, though nonspecifically.
Cystic or subpleural fragile lung changes create the substrate for pneumothorax.
Pneumothorax worsens gas exchange and may force escalation of ventilatory support.
ARDS physiology increases death hazard through refractory hypoxemia and ventilator complications.
Invasive ventilation is a strong marker and mediator of poor outcome in severe PJP.
Air leak complicates oxygenation and ventilation, increasing mortality hazard.
Coinfection or ICU-acquired infection adds sepsis and lung injury pressure.
PJP-associated IRIS can worsen oxygenation despite organism burden decline.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Life-threatening sulfonamide reactions such as SJS/TEN or DRESS should prevent rechallenge.
Renal impairment requires dosing adjustment and monitoring for creatinine rise and hyperkalemia.
Folate antagonism and neonatal bilirubin concerns require pregnancy-specific risk management and folate support.

side_effects.interpretation: Sulfonamide rash or hypersensitivity can confound fever/rash assessment.
Leukopenia or marrow suppression can occur during high-dose therapy.
Thrombocytopenia is a recognized adverse effect.
Trimethoprim can raise measured creatinine by tubular secretion inhibition and can also contribute to true kidney injury.
Trimethoprim can cause hyperkalemia, especially with renal impairment or RAAS blockade.

treatments.context_specific_role: High-potency active anti-Pneumocystis regimen that directly reduces organism burden; downstream improvement in oxygenation is delayed because inflammation and surfactant dysfunction resolve more slowly.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Primaquine can cause severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency.
Primaquine is oral; unreliable absorption reduces active exposure.
Pre-existing or rising methemoglobinemia worsens hypoxemia independent of lung mechanics.

side_effects.interpretation: Primaquine can cause methemoglobinemia, causing persistent low pulse oximetry despite improving lung injury.
Hemolysis risk is highest with G6PD deficiency.
Clindamycin can cause diarrhea and C. difficile colitis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Active regimen when TMP-SMX cannot be used; efficacy depends on safe primaquine use and reliable oral absorption.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pentamidine can worsen kidney injury and electrolyte instability.
Pentamidine can prolong QT and cause dysrhythmia.
Pentamidine can cause hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia.

side_effects.interpretation: Nephrotoxicity is common enough to drive treatment switching.
Pentamidine can produce hyperglycemia after pancreatic beta-cell toxicity.
QT prolongation and arrhythmias require ECG monitoring.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral active regimen when oral absorption is unreliable or TMP-SMX cannot be used, with toxicity monitored as part of the outcome path.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Atovaquone suspension has variable bioavailability and requires food/fat for absorption.
Severe oxygenation failure requires a higher-potency active regimen.

side_effects.interpretation: GI intolerance can reduce adherence and absorption.
Transaminase elevation is possible and should be monitored when baseline hepatic disease exists.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral active regimen with lower potency and absorption dependence; fits mild oxygenation impairment or toxicity-driven switches.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Dapsone can cause hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency.
This oral regimen is less suitable for severe oxygenation failure.

side_effects.interpretation: Dapsone-related methemoglobinemia can mimic persistent pulmonary hypoxemia.
Hemolysis risk is amplified by G6PD deficiency.
Dapsone hypersensitivity or rash can force discontinuation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral active regimen for contexts where TMP-SMX is not usable and oxygenation failure is not severe.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Higher A-a gradient identifies oxygenation failure where dampening inflammation can improve outcome.
Little benefit is expected when oxygenation impairment is absent.
Additional immunosuppression can worsen concurrent untreated infections.

side_effects.interpretation: Steroid-induced hyperglycemia can require active management.
Additional immunosuppression can increase coinfection hazard.
Steroid complications affect treatment tolerability and monitoring intensity.

treatments.context_specific_role: Inflammation-modifying add-on that directly reduces host alveolitis and respiratory failure pressure when oxygenation impairment is clinically meaningful.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ART only modifies the PJP landscape when HIV is the relevant immune-defect context.
Immune restoration can transiently amplify pulmonary inflammation.

side_effects.interpretation: Pulmonary IRIS is uncommon but can worsen respiratory symptoms after initial improvement.

treatments.context_specific_role: Host-immunity intervention for HIV-context PJP that lowers future susceptibility and recurrence while adding a time-limited inflammatory flare hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: No meaningful effect if iatrogenic immunosuppression is not the driver.
Rapid immune restoration can increase pulmonary inflammation.

side_effects.interpretation: Pulmonary inflammatory worsening may occur during immune restoration.

treatments.context_specific_role: Contextual immune-restoration intervention that reduces the host susceptibility mechanism when disease control allows immunosuppression taper.

cd4_below_100.trajectory_modulation: higher organism burden, longer untreated course, higher recurrence risk without prophylaxis

advanced_or_uncontrolled.trajectory_modulation: more subacute symptom duration and higher organism burden; ART becomes a host-immunity treatment context

present.trajectory_modulation: often lower organism burden but more abrupt inflammatory lung injury and higher respiratory failure mortality
raises cell-mediated immune defect; can blunt fever and CRP while allowing severe hypoxemia
higher coinfection hazard, drug interaction burden, and mortality with respiratory failure

effective_prophylaxis.trajectory_modulation: breakthrough disease remains possible with nonadherence, underdosing, poor absorption, or profound immunosuppression

absent_or_interrupted.trajectory_modulation: higher prior probability and recurrence hazard after treatment if immune defect persists

present.trajectory_modulation: lower oxygenation reserve and higher ventilation/mortality hazard

over_65.trajectory_modulation: higher mortality from lower physiologic reserve and comorbidity burden

present.trajectory_modulation: does not define PJP but raises CRP/PCT, worsens hypoxemia, and increases mortality hazard

supportive_care: Oxygen titration with close monitoring for exertional and resting desaturation.
High-flow nasal cannula or noninvasive ventilation for selected hypoxemic patients with careful pneumothorax monitoring.
Lung-protective invasive ventilation when respiratory failure cannot be supported noninvasively.
ABG or equivalent oxygenation assessment to quantify PaO2, P/F ratio, and A-a gradient when hypoxemia is present.
Thin-section chest CT when CXR is normal but suspicion remains or when cystic change, pneumothorax, or alternative diagnoses need evaluation.
Obtain induced sputum or BAL for Pneumocystis PCR/stain while not delaying treatment when clinical suspicion is high.
Check serum beta-D-glucan as a supportive non-specific marker, interpreted alongside host risk and imaging.
Evaluate for bacterial, viral, mycobacterial, CMV, and fungal coinfection when procalcitonin is high, effusion/consolidation is prominent, or treatment response is poor.
Monitor clinical failure by oxygenation trajectory over days 4-8 while accounting for early inflammatory worsening after organism lysis.
Monitor CBC, creatinine, potassium, liver enzymes, glucose, and drug-specific toxicity during anti-Pneumocystis treatment.
Check G6PD before dapsone or primaquine exposure when feasible; choose another regimen if deficient.
Assess methemoglobinemia if hypoxemia persists despite improving imaging or symptoms while receiving dapsone or primaquine.
Drain clinically significant pneumothorax promptly; minimize barotrauma if positive-pressure ventilation is required.
Review immunosuppressive medications and taper only when the underlying disease or graft context allows.
Plan secondary prophylaxis when the immune defect persists after acute treatment.
Coordinate ART timing, drug interactions, and IRIS monitoring when HIV context is present.
